name: Ammisshaddai
title: Father of Ahiezer, leader of the tribe of Dan
summary: Ammishaddai is a biblical figure primarily known as the father of Ahiezer, the appointed leader of the tribe of Dan during Israel's time in the wilderness. His name is theologically charged and likely means "my people are the Almighty" – a confession that links his lineage to God under his ancient title Shaddai. Although Ammishaddai does not appear independently in the narrative, he serves an important function as a patronym: through his name, his son Ahiezer's leadership is identified and legitimized in the census, the camp arrangement, the offerings at the dedication of the tabernacle, and the command of Dan's military force. In this way, Ammishaddai illustrates how kinship and family belonging were fundamental to Israel's social and religious organization during the wilderness period.

keyEvents.title: Ahiezer appointed as leader of Dan
keyEvents.description: Ahiezer, son of Ammisshaddai, was appointed as the leader of the tribe of Dan when Israel was organized in the wilderness at Sinai.

keyEvents.title: The camp and banner of the tribe of Dan
keyEvents.description: Ahiezer, son of Ammisshaddai, led the tribe of Dan in the camp arrangement on the north side of the tabernacle, together with Asher and Naphtali.

keyEvents.title: Offering at the dedication of the altar
keyEvents.description: Ahiezer, son of Ammisshaddai, presented his offering as tribal leader for Dan on the tenth day during the dedication of the tabernacle's altar.

keyEvents.title: Leader over Dan's military force
keyEvents.description: Ahiezer, son of Ammisshaddai, led the military force of the tribe of Dan when Israel broke camp from the wilderness of Sinai.

versions.summary: Ammishaddai was the father of Ahiezer, who served as leader and chief of the tribe of Dan during Israel's wilderness journey. He is known primarily through his son Ahiezer's role in the census and the offerings presented at the dedication of the tabernacle. Ammishaddai is mentioned several times in Numbers as a patronym to identify Ahiezer.

versions.reason: [major] Ammisaddai was not himself a 'leader'. He is only known as the father of Ahiezer. His sole role in the text is as an ancestor/father. The role should be changed to 'ancestor' or 'father'.; [minor] The title 'Father of the Danite tribal leader' is functionally correct, but could have been slightly more precise, for example, 'Father of Ahiezer, the Danite tribal leader'.; [minor] The summary is good, but could briefly mention the meaning of the name Ammisaddai ('my people are the Almighty') to provide greater contextual depth.; [minor] Footnotes are missing. The etymology of the name and its contextual role in Numbers deserve a footnote.

footnotes.text: The name Ammishaddai (Hebrew: עַמִּישַׁדָּי) is composed of 'ammi' (עַמִּי, 'my people') and 'shaddai' (שַׁדָּי, 'the Almighty'). The divine name Shaddai ('El Shaddai') is especially linked to the patriarchal narratives (Gen 17:1; Exod 6:3) and represents a very ancient tradition in Israelite faith. The inclusion of this divine name in a personal name from the wilderness journey testifies to the continuity of theological tradition from the time of the patriarchs.

The use of patronymics (father's names) as an identifier was widespread practice in ancient Israel and throughout the ancient Near East. In Numbers, the form 'X son of Y' is used systematically to identify tribal leaders, underscoring the central role of kinship and tribal affiliation for social organization. Ammishaddai is known exclusively through his role as the patronym for his son Ahiezer.

Ahiezer, son of Ammishaddai, was the tenth tribal leader who presented his offering at the dedication of the tabernacle's altar (Num 7:66). The systematic order of the offerings, where each tribal leader had their own day, reflects the camp arrangement in Num 2 and emphasizes that all twelve tribes held equal dignity and access to God's sanctuary.

The tribe of Dan, which Ahiezer led, was positioned on the north side of the tabernacle together with Asher and Naphtali (Num 2:25). This placement in the camp arrangement had both practical and symbolic significance: the tabernacle stood at the center with the tribes surrounding it, expressing God's presence in the midst of His people.
